inline.s: Xu Zhijing, given name Yehu, was born in Pengze, Jiangxi. In the Guichen year of the Guangxu reign he won the jinshi degree and served at the Hanlin Academy for eight years, retiring into seclusion after the restoration. In 1917 he turned his heart to the Buddhas and devoted himself wholly to the Pure Land. In 1922 he went to Putuo to pay homage to the Bodhisattva and called upon Master Yinguang, seeking refuge and receiving the Dharma name Zhijing. From that time he kept a long vegetarian fast. He resolved to compile three works, the "Eulogy on the Spiritual Responses of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva," "A General Record of Karmic Response in History," and "A Buddhist Discourse for Deliverance from Calamity," completing and circulating them in turn; all among monks and laity who held right understanding marveled that his Buddhist insight was profound and his literary craft refined. In 1936 he again asked Master Yinguang to bestow the bodhisattva precepts. Though Zhijing was broadly versed in scripture and doctrine, he was in all things like the simplest man or woman, earnestly reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. He bowed to every monk he met and paid homage to every Buddha image he saw. Zhijing was frail and often unwell. In May 1938 he took refuge amid the troubles at Huanglong Temple on Guling, Mount Lu, and lay sick. By the intercalary seventh month his condition had somewhat healed. On the first day of the ninth month he summoned Yao Banseng, who lodged with him in the temple, and entrusted him with his affairs after death. Then he smiled and said, "This morning I dreamed that the Buddha came, adorned all about with jeweled netting, radiant with the marks of perfection and light. He said to me, I have come to see you. I at once bowed to him. After a while I woke. Was it not the World-Honored One's compassion, coming especially to comfort me? If he would only manifest his welcome and allow me to be reborn by virtue of past karma, what great good fortune that would be!" Having spoken he joined his palms and said, "We shall meet again in the West!" From then on he made no further sound, only single-mindedly and silently reciting the Buddha's name. At seven o'clock on the morning of the third day he passed serenely to the West. His whole body grew cold, yet the crown of his head remained warm. When placed in the coffin his whole body was soft as cotton, exactly like an old monk settled in meditation. His countenance was radiant, more so than in life. This is what is meant by the faculties at ease, right mindfulness clear, the relinquishing of life serene, as though entering samadhi. His body was kept in the temple and the Buddha's name recited for seven days, then cremated in accordance with the Dharma; his ashes were preserved at Huanglong Temple. He was sixty-three.

Xia Lianju was eager to learn from youth and broadly versed in the whole of the canon. He deeply probed the principle of mind and was accomplished in many arts. In mid-life he quietly studied the Buddhist scriptures. From the doctrinal schools to the teaching, from the exoteric to the esoteric, he penetrated them all without obstruction, gathering everything into the Pure Land. In the Yichou year, when the warlord Zhang Zongchang governed Shandong, he was charged with a fabricated crime, his property was confiscated, and an order was issued for his arrest, so he fled to Japan to escape the calamity. Returning after a year, he closed himself in retreat at Tianjin. His small room held only an image of Amitabha Buddha; with single mind he devoutly held the sacred name, stilling thought and cutting off deliberation, applying himself to the Way with utmost dedication. Thus he passed ten years. Through the union of his practice and the Buddha's power, auspicious signs appeared again and again; he saw the Buddha and saw light, yet never revealed this to others. He had a verse: "One scroll of the six-character sutra / Breaks open ten years of darkness. / People say that I recite the Buddha; / I say the Buddha is reciting me. / Through clouds of delusion and fog of dust passing on, / In a clear pool I see the round moon's reflection a perfect circle." In the September

18 Incident broke out, and the national crisis was at its height. The monks and laity of Beijing repeatedly and earnestly invited him, so he came to the capital and settled beside the Drum Tower. He pursued the Way with keen resolve and gave himself wholly to teaching, widely praising the Mahayana and proclaiming the Pure Land school, tireless in instructing others, the same decade after decade. Those seeking the Way and inquiring into doctrine filled his courtyard day by day; those obtaining the benefit of the Dharma were beyond counting. Some attained clear realization and saw their own nature; some at rebirth stood and departed; some showed auspicious signs at rebirth; some left the world and became monastics. As for those who, on hearing the teaching, awakened faith and cleansed their hearts toward goodness, they were more than could be reckoned. In deep winter of the Yisi year, aged eighty-three, he said one day to those about him, "My great matter is accomplished; I am resolved to leave this defiled world." At that time his spirit was vigorous. The essential Dharma he taught and the states revealed in his practice were for the most part things he had never before spoken of. Ten days later he showed a slight illness. At night his family attended him and heard him reciting the Buddha's name without break. Suddenly they heard a single ringing utterance; startled, they looked, and in that very name of myriad virtues he passed serenely to rebirth. Right mindfulness was clear, and he went as soon as he said he would. He entered the sea of Amitabha's vow, a model for students; how true it is! Several verses on mindful recitation from his retreat years survive in transmission.

Chen Wuwo, style name Faxiang, lived in Shanghai though his ancestral home was Qiantang. He served as editor of the "Pacific News" and the "Republic Daily" among other publications. Deeply learned in Chinese letters, he founded the New World News Agency and acted as its head. The layman Chen Baixu guided him to faith in Buddhism. On reading the "Protection of Life Picture Book" he resolved to become a vegetarian. To spread the Buddha Dharma he opened the Great Dharma Wheel Bookstore, circulating Buddhist books. He also compiled and printed the monthly "Awakened Sentience." The monthly's contents were substantial and lively, and the editing and selection of manuscripts Chen Wuwo personally undertook. It was published for more than ten years, with subscribers at home and abroad. He also wrote "All Are Rejoicing" and "Strange Dreams of Rebirth," works that accord with principle and with the capacity of beings, much favored by readers. At forty-two he lost his wife and never married again. Wuwo firmly believed in the Pure Land. He once told his friend Dou Cunwo, "I have read the Master Zhongfeng's

Three Rites of Mind and found it deeply effective." Every dawn at cockcrow he rose, and his worship and recitation were diligent. In dealing with the world he was honest toward others, a kindly elder. On November 3, 1967 he passed away in illness while reciting the Buddha's name, aged eighty-four. His son Xinchun, style name Nianci, was also versed in the Dharma and wrote "Nianci's Essays." Resolute in the Pure Land, he passed away early of a frail body.

Zhang Dalang, of Dapan Village, Huaiyuan, Anhui, was illiterate but most filial to his mother, earning his living as a stone mason. He received the practice of reciting the Buddha's name from Xu Benxiao, a man of his district; his wife tried hard to stop him, but he was not moved. Before long his wife died, and he applied himself with single mind, bowing and reciting day and night without rest. He did this for seven years. In the year 1920, as the Mid-Autumn Festival approached, he showed a slight illness. He said to his mother, "After I leave I shall surely come first to deliver you; do not grieve." His mother, who already kept a vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha's name, also urged her son: "Recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and seek rebirth." At noon on the thirteenth day of the eighth month he instructed his younger brother Genlang: "From now on you must serve our old mother well. I am about to go. The heavenly music of the West has come to welcome me; do you hear it?" Having spoken, he lit incense, sat cross-legged, joined his palms, and passed away. At that moment heavenly music suddenly sounded in the sky, like a small trumpet, its tone so sweet as to be beyond description. Besides the heavenly music there were two lamps as large as basins, waving and rippling, seen by all the assembled people for about two hours before they disappeared. People outside the village all heard the sound of the heavenly music above Dapan Village, and several hundred came to watch. Yet the moment they entered the village the sound ceased, while the villagers still heard it. Not one of the onlookers failed to sigh in wonder. Dalang was then thirty years old. Years later his mother lay ill and said to those around her, "My son Dalang has come to welcome me," and so passed away. Wang Kunru of Dama Works in Yujiao County, Anhui, wrote to Master Yinguang about Dalang's affair. The master replied, "A matter as extraordinary as mason Zhang's must mean there are people in that place who earnestly recite the Buddha's name. You should go and inquire and confirm it, in order to encourage faith." Wang Kunru then wrote to Huaiyuan to ask, and received replies from four gentlemen of the village, Pan Weisheng, Hu Jiachun, Zheng Guangyi, and Pan Fuyi, testifying that they had all seen and heard it together and that it was indeed beyond doubt. The mason Zhang was a man who could not read a single character, yet the moment he heard the practice of reciting the Buddha's name he believed, accepted, and practiced it. Though he met with setbacks, his resolve was never weakened. With the three requisites of faith, vow, and practice complete, after seven years of diligent practice he left the burning house. The entry is easy and the success swift, all the more confirming that the Pure Land method answers the capacity of these times.

Zhou Zishan, named Yuying, was the eldest grandson of the great merchant Zhou Fujiu of Ji'an, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was raised by his grandmother, Lady Tan. Naturally clever and fond of learning, he was kind and gentle, his heart empty as a valley. Though born into a wealthy house he had not the slightest trace of arrogance or extravagance. In office he was known for uprightness and loyalty. When colleagues, relatives, friends, and even servants erred, he never turned a harsh word or angry look on them. When he retired into seclusion he closed his door and nurtured his own virtue. On casually reading the Buddhist canon he knew that the Buddha Dharma is the root of all things in the world, and that the welfare of society and the deliverance of all beings rest upon it. Thereupon he took refuge under Master Dixian and received the Dharma name Zhizang. From then on he kept a long fast and recited the Buddha's name, refraining from killing and nurturing life, frugal in his own living. To friends and relations who asked for help he never tired of responding. He relieved the hungry and cold as a matter of course, generously aiding every good undertaking. All the worldly good he did he dedicated, with a great bodhi-mind, toward the West. In 1932, the Renshen year, he reached the age of knowing his mandate. On the eighth day of the fourth month, which fell on the Buddha's birthday, at seven in the morning he showed a slight illness. Feeling pain in his back and waist, he asked someone to pat him gently for relief. He himself sat cross-legged facing west, single-mindedly reciting "Amitabha Buddha" in a clear voice. After a long time his voice gradually lowered, and he passed away. The person patting his back, seeing him long still and silent, felt for his breath and knew he had already relinquished his body and gone to rebirth. A rare fragrance filled the room and did not disperse for five days.

Fu Chunpu, given name Chuan, was from Dongguo Village, Qingjiang County, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was educated by his mother, Lady Nie, who in her hardship kept her honor and raised him. He studied law, government, and police science, and served in posts as county-office clerk and school principal. His mother had long served the Bodhisattva Guanyin, keeping a vegetarian fast and reciting the Buddha's name. In 1928, because of his mother's illness, he vowed to make a pilgrimage to Putuo; his mother's illness soon healed. So in the ninth month of 1931 he went to Putuo to fulfill his vow. Paying homage at the Cave of the Dharma Sound, he felt the Bodhisattva appear in a white robe holding a pure vase and a willow branch. He further sought to know his past lives and saw a mendicant in tattered clothing, and so understood that the wheel of rebirth was no illusion. He called upon Master Yinguang at Baoguo Temple in Suzhou and first heard the essentials of the Pure Land teaching. From then on he believed, vowed, and recited, advancing without slack. He also took refuge under Master Desen and received the Dharma name Chuanchuan. In 1933 he served as lecturer-in-chief of the Lujiang Recitation Grove, guiding and encouraging many followers. His family had long been poor and he was frail and often ill. That spring he dreamed that the Bodhisattva Guanyin spoke to him, setting the time in the seventh month. After the Ullambana assembly he fell ill and, with single mind, recited the Buddha's name, forgetting his suffering. On the twenty-third, relatives and friends aided his recitation; he lost consciousness, then revived after a while. He invited Master Daren and entrusted him with his cremation. On the twenty-sixth he lapsed again and the family wept around him. The layman smiled and stopped them, saying, "Why do you weep? I shall be reborn on the festival day of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva." At the appointed time, sitting upright in a chair, he formed the Amitabha mudra, gazed fixedly on the Buddha image, and passed away peacefully. His whole body was cold yet the crown of his head alone was warm, his face lovely and radiant beyond his living looks. On the second day of the intercalary seventh month the abbot Dasong of Tonghui Temple in Zhangshu Town and Master Daren came to attend to his encoffining; he sat cross-legged with palms joined, exactly like a living man. The day before had been great wind and rain, yet when at the hour of Zi the fire was lit the sky suddenly brightened, and a rare fragrance filled the air, neither orchid nor sandalwood. A beam of white light issued from the coffin and shot toward the West. He was forty-eight.

Bei Zushan, styled Youwei, was a native of Suzhou. Naturally quick, he was filial to his mother. She was blind, and he licked her eyes and restored her sight. His elder sister married into the Yan family, but both husband and wife died young, leaving one son and two daughters, small and helpless. Zushan raised and supported them all, even seeing them through their higher schooling. Among his brothers and friends any who met sudden hardship he helped with all he had, never a grudging look. In his prime he drifted through officialdom, serving as head of the Nanjing Electric Works, confidential secretary to Song Ziwen, and customs director. In his forties, differing in opinion from those in power, he retired home and gave himself to the study of body and mind, life and nature. He first practiced the Daoist arts of breathing and guidance, then studied the esoteric school. Nearing the age of knowing his mandate he at last heard from a teacher the Pure Land method of holding the name, rejoiced to have found his true home, and cast aside all his former learning and practice. One phrase, "Amitabha," he held single-mindedly. Even when distant guests came or pressing matters arose, he would not come out to respond until his daily recitation was complete. In the autumn of 1936 he suddenly fell ill. Knowing the affinity with the Pure Land had ripened, he arranged in advance all the matters of his final moments. Fearing that his wife's deep worldly love would bring tears, he had already moved her to another room and let her know nothing. Besides inviting several Dharma friends to lead the assisting recitation, he kept only his eldest daughter beside him to attend to him, and earnestly charged the household, "You must not weep or make a disturbance. For eight hours after my death you must not touch the body. Everything must be done as the book "Companion for the Final Journey" prescribes." All other relatives, friends, and his children were refused seeing him. With single mind he recited the Buddha's name, resolved on rebirth. When his illness was grave, his brother-in-law Zhao came to see him and, seeing him so ill, could not hold back his tears. Zushan laughed and consoled him instead, "All our lives you and I have recited the Buddha's name and cultivated the Pure Land precisely for rebirth at a time like this. This is a great and joyous matter; how can we act like worldly sons and daughters?" Throughout the illness his mind remained clear. On the twelfth day of the ninth month at the hour of Hai, he joined his palms, sat cross-legged upon his bed, and passed away reciting the Buddha's name. He was fifty-two.

Nie Yunsheng, named Chuanceng, was a native of Qingjiang, Jiangxi. Losing his father in childhood, he was raised by his mother, grave and fond of learning. He passed the jinshi examination in the Guichen year of the Guangxu reign and took office in Hubei. Soon after the death of his eldest brother he returned home and was elected a member of the provincial assembly. He fully discharged his duty of remonstrance, fearing no one in power. Before long he flung up his sleeve and withdrew. In life he loved classical prose, yet would never write carelessly unless it served the world. In later years he studied the Buddhist canon, taking up the Lotus, Shurangama, Diamond, and Perfect Enlightenment scriptures and reciting them in turn, while gathering all into the five Pure Land sutras. He kept a long fast and a fixed daily recitation. In the Dingchou year he established the Gaoyu Recitation Grove, and often went to other recitation groves to speak, transforming many. In the summer of Jihai he was troubled by repeated diarrhea. Set resolutely on returning to the West, he no longer sought the help of medicine. By the tenth month his decline was graver still. Knowing his time had come, he dictated his last will and invited monks, relatives, and friends, leading his children and grandchildren in reciting the Buddha's name. As he sank ever weaker he still recited silently through clenched teeth. Without any pain, right mindfulness clear, he relinquished his life serenely as though entering samadhi, his features as if living. Yunsheng was born in the Jisi year of the eighth year of the Tongzhi reign and returned to the West on the first day of the eleventh month of the Jimao year, 1939, at the age of seventy-one. His work "Poems, Essays and Diary from the Hall of Mending Prajna" much clarifies the meaning of the Pure Land teaching, and is kept in his home.

Zhao Xiude, of Xingtai city in Hebei, was most filial to his mother, honest with all men, and of a pure, thickhearted nature. He took refuge in the Three Jewels and strictly kept the five precepts. In midwinter of 1938 his mother fell gravely ill and the whole family recited the Buddha's name. At her end she charged Xiude with great earnestness, "Recite the Buddha's name well. Within three years, do not let your recitation stop." Having given this charge, she lay in the auspicious posture and passed away serenely. Three hours later her body was soft, the crown of her head warm, and her face suffused with radiance. After his mother's death Xiude did all things in accordance with the rites. He also obeyed his mother's command: for three years, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, he never ceased reciting. Every dawn at cockcrow he rose and went beneath the pagoda of Perfect Light, walking around it to the right while reciting the Buddha's name. When he walked, if bricks or stones blocked the road he would kick them clean away so as not to hinder travelers. When a fast day came he went to the Buddha hall of Kaiyuan Temple and struck the bell and lit the lamps, tending the incense. Whoever he met he urged to recite the Buddha's name. His word of exhortation ran, "Recite the Buddha's name! Recite the Buddha's name! The Land of Bliss is our own home." In holding the Buddha's name he was utterly diligent; in keeping his mother's command he was wholly sincere and careful. By November 1941 he said repeatedly, "My mother's command is fulfilled; I shall soon return. But because my past karma cannot be escaped, I must suffer the pain of illness." Presently he showed a slight ailment, and when it came on his chest and back ached, just as he had said. One day, rousing himself despite his illness, he went to Kaiyuan Temple to bow before the Buddha. On finishing he returned home, closed his eyes and mouth, and neither looked nor spoke. Smiling alone, he sat upright in a chair, his left hand making the gesture of counting beads while reciting the Buddha's name, and passed away. Four hours later the crown of his head was still warm, and a strange fragrance lingered for days. It was the first day of the twelfth month of 1941. He was fifty-six.

Yu Mingsheng, of Gaoting on Daishan, Zhejiang, was a farmer, simple and goodhearted. Whenever a dispute arose in his village he would come forward and settle it. To aid the imperiled, relieve the afflicted, and bring things to a good end he took pleasure as his own duty. Yet he did not know what the Buddha Dharma might be. His son Dingyong, who from youth embraced the Buddhas, took refuge under Master Yuanying, devoted himself to the Pure Land, and founded a lay Buddhist association in the countryside to guide the people in reciting the Buddha's name. Though Mingsheng was influenced by this, his practice was not yet earnest. On the twenty-third day of the first month of 1942 he fell slightly ill. After seven days the illness grew worse. Dingyong then gathered fellow lay devotees and led the family in devout assisting recitation. After a day and a night the illness improved and his mind cleared. Dingyong consoled him kindly and told him of the excellence of rebirth through the Buddha-name. Mingsheng came to understanding with joy, let go of everything, and with single mind recited the Buddha's name. He also told the assembly, "Recite the four-character name." The people did as he said. On the morning of the second day of the second month he said to his son, "I want my hair cut, a bath, and fresh clothes." Dingyong asked, "Father, can you be reborn in the West?" He answered, "Yes!" — the words firm and forceful. The assembly continued their aiding recitation, the Buddha's name unbroken. At midnight of the next day Mingsheng told the company, "I have already seen Amitabha Buddha, a lotus in his hand." On saying this he began to rise as if to seat himself on the lotus throne, and himself struck the small bell and recited the Buddha's name loudly. After an hour his voice gradually faded; his younger brother Mingmao and others recited at his side. They told him, "The ten final recitations at death surely attain rebirth." Mingsheng gathered his spirit again, joined his palms, and recited "Namo Amitabha Buddha." At the eighth utterance his voice suddenly fell and his breath stopped. A quarter of an hour later he revived, laughed aloud before the company, and said again and again, "I am overjoyed!" Then he passed away serenely. At the encoffining the next day his limbs were soft and his face rosy as in life. He was forty-nine.

Zhu Shiseng, given name Qi. In his early years he took refuge under Master Dixian and received the Dharma name Xianjia. Later he took refuge under Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Zhirui. His father was a farmer; his mother, Lady Yang, was fond of helping others. Shiseng, schooled in his youth by his family, was kind, honest, and plain. He served long as stationmaster of Wusong on the Shanghai-Nanjing Railway. In 1922 he took the lead in establishing the World Buddhist Lay Association and served as vice-chairman. He oversaw the expansion of the association's main hall and quarters, planning and rushing about at great pains. In 1931, the July

7 Incident broke out, and there were many refugees in Shanghai, in hunger and cold. Shiseng, in consultation with Dharma friends, raised funds to set up a Buddhist society for relieving the cold and did his utmost in relief works. For all the cold, destitute, and hidden poor he made thorough investigation and dispensed monthly aid. In protecting the Dharma and relieving beings he exhausted his heart's blood. In later years, worn by overwork, he was often afflicted with illness. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the old calendar, 1942, when Master Miaozhen of Lingyan heard that Shiseng was gravely ill, he came personally to his sickbed and gave detailed instruction, charging him to "let go all ties, raise right mindfulness, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and seek rebirth in the West." Shiseng was deeply moved and put it earnestly into practice. By nine in the morning of the eleventh, as fellow members of the association were aiding his recitation, his son Yongjun asked his father, "Can you still recite the Buddha's name in your heart?" He nodded and said, "Yes! My heart has long since reached the West; the Buddha-name recitation truly does not come to nothing." He then asked for a pen and wrote the few characters "Your father is surely bound for the West." He fingered his beads, his lips and teeth moving faintly, reciting the Buddha's name without ceasing. By the hour of noon he passed serenely into rebirth in the West.
